firmware.summary: The rover starts its own Wi-Fi access point and serves a touch-joystick page at http://192.168.4.1; the phone sends throttle and turn about ten times a second. The firmware mixes these into left and right wheel speeds and drives the DRV8833 with 20 kHz PWM capped at 75 % duty, with ramping to keep start surges down. If commands stop for 0.5 s, the motors coast and the driver is put to sleep; this failsafe runs in its own 10 ms task, so a stalled web request cannot delay it. Battery voltage is read through the 100k/33k divider on GPIO3: below 6.8 V the red LED flashes, and below 6.4 V for 2 s the motors lock out until the pack is back above 7.0 V. Green blinks while waiting for the phone and is solid while it is driving.

pins.connectsTo: R3 330 ohm -> D1 bi-colour LED green anode
pins.note: Active high. Blink = waiting for phone, solid = phone linked.

pins.connectsTo: R3 330 ohm -> D1 bi-colour LED red anode
pins.note: Active high. Flash = low battery warning, solid = battery cut-off.

pins.connectsTo: R1 100k/33k divider tap with C2 100 nF
pins.note: 11 dB attenuation, VBAT = pin voltage x 133/33. Not a strapping pin.
Left motor forward, LEDC 20 kHz 10-bit, max 75 % duty.
Low = driver asleep, outputs off. Driven low first thing at boot and whenever the motors are not allowed to run.

files.content:
#pragma once
// Pin map, matches the design's connections.
// Strapping pins GPIO2, GPIO8 and GPIO9 are deliberately left unused.

#define PIN_LED_GREEN   0   // D1 green anode via R3 330R, active high
#define PIN_LED_RED     1   // D1 red anode via R3 330R, active high
#define PIN_VBAT_SENSE  3   // ADC1_CH3, 100k/33k divider tap + 100 nF
#define PIN_AIN1        4   // DRV8833 AIN1 (left motor forward)
#define PIN_AIN2        5   // DRV8833 AIN2 (left motor reverse)
#define PIN_BIN1        6   // DRV8833 BIN1 (right motor forward)
#define PIN_BIN2        7   // DRV8833 BIN2 (right motor reverse)
#define PIN_NSLEEP      10  // DRV8833 nSLEEP, low = outputs off

#pragma once
#include <stdint.h>

// ---- Wi-Fi access point (change the password before use) ----
#define AP_SSID_PREFIX   "Rover-"
#define AP_PASSWORD      "rover1234"   // WPA2 needs at least 8 characters
#define AP_CHANNEL       6
#define AP_MAX_CLIENTS   1             // only one phone may drive at a time

// ---- Motor PWM ----
#define PWM_FREQ_HZ      20000
#define PWM_BITS         10
#define PWM_FULL         1023
#define DUTY_MAX         767           // 75 % cap: 8.4 V pack -> about 6.3 V on a 6 V motor
#define DUTY_MIN         205           // 20 %: roughly where an N20 starts to turn
#define CMD_DEADBAND     5             // commands under 5 % count as stop
#define TURN_GAIN_PCT    70            // tames steering so the rover is not twitchy
#define INVERT_LEFT      false         // flip if a wheel runs backwards
#define INVERT_RIGHT     false

// ---- Control loop ----
#define CONTROL_PERIOD_MS  10
#define CMD_TIMEOUT_MS     500         // motors stop if no command for this long
#define ACCEL_STEP         4           // % per tick: 0 -> 100 % in 250 ms, limits start surge
#define DECEL_STEP         10          // % per tick: 100 -> 0 % in 100 ms

// ---- Battery (2S Li-ion through 100k / 33k divider) ----
#define DIV_R_TOP_K        100
#define DIV_R_BOTTOM_K     33
#define VBAT_CAL_PERMILLE  1000        // trim after comparing with a multimeter
#define VBAT_WARN_MV       6800        // red LED starts flashing
#define VBAT_CUTOFF_MV     6400        // motors locked out
#define VBAT_RECOVER_MV    7000        // clears warning and lock-out
#define VBAT_CUTOFF_HOLD_MS 2000       // must stay low this long, rides through start sag
#define VBAT_SAMPLE_MS     20

build: Install PlatformIO Core (pip install platformio) or the PlatformIO extension for VS Code.
Put the files in a project folder with the generated platformio.ini, then build with: pio run
Remove the JP1 3V3 jumper before plugging in USB so the buck and the USB regulator never fight, then connect the dev board's USB-C port.
Watch the console with: pio device monitor -b 115200
Unplug USB, refit JP1, and switch the rover on from the rocker switch for battery use.
test: USB only, JP1 removed, battery switch off, wheels off the ground: the console should print 'Rover booting' and a VBAT near 0 mV, the red LED should be solid, and the motors must not move.

Join the Wi-Fi network 'Rover-XXXX' (password rover1234) with a phone and open http://192.168.4.1; the page should show the voltage and 'battery empty, motors locked', and dragging the joystick must not move the wheels.

Still on USB with JP1 removed, switch the battery on with charged cells: within a second the red LED should go out, green should go solid while the page is open, and the page voltage should match a multimeter on J3 pin 1 within about 0.1 V (trim VBAT_CAL_PERMILLE in config.h if not).
With the wheels still off the ground, push the joystick slightly forward: both wheels should turn forward slowly. If one runs backwards, set INVERT_LEFT or INVERT_RIGHT, or swap that motor's plug.
Push the joystick right: the left wheel should run faster than the right; at full right with no throttle the wheels should counter-rotate.
Scope or meter AIN1 (GPIO4) at full forward: 20 kHz with duty no higher than 75 %.
Failsafe: hold full forward, then turn the phone's Wi-Fi off or close the browser tab. The wheels must stop within about half a second and green should go back to blinking.
Release the joystick: the wheels should stop within about 0.1 s and the knob should re-centre.

Low battery: feed J3 from a bench supply (current limit 1 A) instead of the pack. Drop to 6.7 V: the red LED flashes. Drop to 6.3 V for more than 2 s: red goes solid and the motors stop. Raise above 7.0 V: back to green and drivable.
Finally, refit JP1, unplug USB, put the rover on the floor and drive gently; check that the 2 A fuse holds during quick reversals.
assumptions: The brief's 'walking robot' label is ignored, as the design notes say; this firmware is for the two-wheel rover that the parts and connections describe.
The design only says 'phone-controlled' over Wi-Fi/BLE. I chose a Wi-Fi access point with a built-in web joystick so no phone app or extra library is needed; BLE is not used.
The AP is 'Rover-' plus the last two MAC bytes, password 'rover1234', channel 6, at 192.168.4.1, limited to one client. Change the password in config.h.
Control uses plain HTTP GET /d?x=&y= at about 10 Hz (x = turn, y = throttle, -100..100), not WebSocket; the reply carries battery voltage and state.
Motors coast and the DRV8833 is put to sleep if no command arrives for 500 ms.

DRV8833 channel A (AIN1/AIN2, GPIO4/5) is the left motor and channel B (BIN1/BIN2, GPIO6/7) is the right; the design does not say which is which. INVERT_LEFT / INVERT_RIGHT in config.h fix wiring polarity.

Drive is fast decay (one input PWM, the other low), so every input low means coast. PWM is 20 kHz, 10-bit, hard-capped at 75 % duty as the design states; the cap is fixed and not compensated for battery voltage.
Minimum running duty is 20 % and the joystick deadband is 5 %; both are guesses for N20 100:1 motors and can be tuned in config.h.
Ramp is 0 to full in 250 ms and full to 0 in 100 ms, to keep two motors' start current under the 2 A fuse. Turn gain is 70 %.

The Pololu DRV8833 carrier pulls nSLEEP high on its own, so the driver is awake for the few milliseconds before the firmware runs; its inputs have internal pull-downs, so the motors coast in that window.
Battery thresholds: warning at 6.8 V, cut-off at 6.4 V (from the design) held for 2 s to ride through motor sag, recovery at 7.0 V. The warning and recovery levels and the hold time are my choices.
Battery reading uses the ESP32-C3 factory ADC calibration (analogReadMilliVolts) at 11 dB attenuation and the nominal 100k/33k ratio, with a trim constant in config.h.
At cut-off the firmware only locks the motors and shows red; it does not deep-sleep. The 2S BMS is relied on for final over-discharge protection.
With no battery (USB only) VBAT reads about 0 V, so the motors stay locked and the LED is solid red; this is intended.

LED meanings: green blinking = ready and waiting for the phone, green solid = commands arriving, red flashing = low battery, red solid = cut-off. The design only says green for link/ready and red for low battery.
The serial console is 115200 baud on the dev board's USB-UART bridge (UART0); GPIO20/21 are left to it. Strapping pins GPIO2, GPIO8 and GPIO9 are unused.
No task watchdog is enabled. The failsafe relies on the 10 ms control task, which runs at higher priority than the web server loop.
Platform is pinned to espressif32@6.9.0 (Arduino core 2.0.x); the PWM code also compiles against core 3.x. No external libraries are used.
Nothing here has been compiled or run on hardware; treat the bench tests as the first real check.
